tier_reason: README shows go test -bench output for fastrand.Uint32n and RNG.Uint32n against math/rand Int31n and rand.New(...).Int31n at GOMAXPROCS=1/2/4; the benchmark code (fastrand_timing_test.go) is public, but no Go version or CPU model is given (only goos linux / goarch amd64), so first-party with partial methodology.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: go test -bench=. with GOMAXPROCS=1, 2 and 4 (goos linux, goarch amd64); Go version not stated; benchmarks in fastrand_timing_test.go
corrections.caveats: Go package, not callable from C++. README benchmark output has no CPU model or Go version. The win is about lock contention in Go's global math/rand of that era: per a WebSearch snippet of the Go blog post 'Evolving the Go Standard Library with math/rand/v2' (go.dev blocked here), Go 1.20 replaced the mutex-protected global generator with a per-thread wyrand generator for programs that do not call rand.Seed, so the multi-CPU scaling gap is likely gone on current Go. Single-CPU gain over math/rand Int31n is small (29.7 vs 31.8 ns/op); the larger single-CPU gain is per-goroutine RNG.Uint32n 6.50 vs rand.New(...).Int31n 17.9 ns/op.

notes: Numbers match README exactly. Metadata checked on github.com: MIT, 206 stars, 17 forks, not archived or a fork, last commit 2021-09-15 (abandoned). The Go 1.20 math/rand change comes from a search snippet, not an opened page.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README (ms, lower is better): Xrandom (Xorshift32) 627 / 640 / 391 versus dart:math Random 895 / 929 / 662 for nextInt / nextDouble / nextBool; about 1.43x, 1.45x and 1.69x faster (derived from page data). Xorshift128, Xorshift64, Mulberry32, Xorshift128p and Splitmix64 also beat Random on all three calls; Qrandom/Drandom (Xoshiro128pp) 933 / 1219 / 398 and Xoshiro256pp 1138 / 1182 / 406 are slower than Random for nextInt and nextDouble but faster for nextBool.

tier_reason: results17.txt is raw JMH 1.37 output on OpenJDK 17.0.2+8 comparing built-in nextGaussian against the library's ziggurat, and the benchmark source (experiment/timing17/src/main/java/org/cicirello/experiments/ziggurat/TimeZigguratVersusJavaBuiltin.java) and pom.xml are public, but no CPU model is stated in the results, the timing17 README or the repo README; the arXiv report (2405.19493) is a preprint and its host was blocked, so first-party tier C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: results17.txt (JMH avgt, ns/op): Random 103.037 built-in versus 17.393 ziggurat; ThreadLocalRandom 88.774 built-in versus 10.901 ziggurat; SplittableRandom 8.927 built-in versus 10.089 ziggurat (built-in faster). About 5.9x and 8.1x faster for Random and ThreadLocalRandom (derived from page data). The same run's wrappedThreadLocalRandom benchmark (ThreadLocalRandom wrapped as a java.util.random.RandomGenerator so Java 17's own modified ziggurat is used) took 10.392 ns/op, slightly faster than the library's 10.901.
corrections.caveats: Java, not callable from C++; the gain is against Java's legacy polar-method nextGaussian, not a C++ facility. On Java 17+ the JDK's own modified ziggurat (RandomGenerator default nextGaussian, used by SplittableRandom and reachable for ThreadLocalRandom by wrapping it as a RandomGenerator) matches or beats this library in the same JMH run (8.927 vs 10.089 and 10.392 vs 10.901 ns/op), so the win only holds against the legacy Random/ThreadLocalRandom/SecureRandom methods or on Java 11-16. Benchmark code and raw JMH output are public but no CPU model is given (JDK path in the output is a Windows path). The arXiv report 2405.19493 was not opened (arXiv and reports.cicirello.org blocked); a search snippet says Java 17's modified ziggurat is faster than this implementation for the PRNGs that support it. README says the library has been absorbed into cicirello/rho-mu (Java 25+).
